To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HCN1- and HCN2- knockout mice have normal transduction currents, and mice expressing a dominant-negative mutant form HCN2 have normal transduction current.
HCN1-3 subunits are expressed in the mouse inner ear but do not localize in the hair bundles, and that HCN channel antagonists do not block hair cell mechanotransduction.
HCN subunits do not appear to be components of the hair cell mechanotransduction channel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of hearing and balance.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the conversion of sound into electrical signals in hair cells of auditory and vestibular organs.
the mechanism of hearing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data presented here provide evidence that HCN subunit proteins are not required for the function of the transduction channels in hair cells of mice.
the HCN channel is not a component of the hair cell mechanotransduction complex.
the hair cell transducer is not a HCN channel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HCN family of voltage-gated ion channels does not contribute to mechanotransduction currents in hair cells.
the transduction channels in the mouse inner ear are not HCN channels.
the HCN channel subunit family is not required for mechanosensation in hair cells of either the mouse cochlea or vestibular system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HCNs are not required for hair cell mechanotransduction and that the molecular composition of the transduction complex remains elusive.
the molecular identity of the hair cell mechanotransduction channel remains unknown.
we found no evidence that the HCN subunits that were examined were required for mechanotansduction in the mouse inner ear.
